leetcode.prompt: An array is sorted and contains duplicates. A standard binary search returns index 3 for the target. What guarantees that index 3 is the FIRST occurrence?

options.text: Nothing — a standard binary search returns an arbitrary matching index
options.why: Correct. On a hit the loop stops, and which of the equal elements it landed on depends on how the midpoints fell. Finding the first occurrence requires recording the hit and continuing to search the left half.

options.text: The array being sorted guarantees it
options.why: Sortedness only guarantees the duplicates are adjacent. It says nothing about which one the midpoint sequence happened to reach.

options.text: It is the first if the array length is odd
options.why: Parity of the length has no bearing on where the midpoints land relative to a run of duplicates.

options.text: Binary search always returns the leftmost match
options.why: That is true only of a variant written to continue leftward after a hit. The textbook version returns as soon as it matches.

leetcode.prompt: What is the time complexity of inserting n elements one by one into a binary heap?

options.text: O(n log n)
options.why: Correct. Each insertion sifts up through at most log n levels, and there are n of them. Note this differs from heapify on an existing array, which is O(n).

options.text: O(n)
options.why: O(n) is build-heap applied to an array already in memory, using sift-down from the middle. Repeated insertion does not get that bound.

options.text: O(log n)
options.why: That is the cost of a single insertion, not of n of them.

options.text: O(n²)
options.why: That would require each insertion to cost O(n). A heap's height is logarithmic, so a sift-up cannot walk more than log n levels.

leetcode.prompt: Why must every rotten cell be enqueued before the first BFS step in the rotting-oranges problem?

options.text: Because all rotten cells spread simultaneously in the same minute
options.why: Correct. The clock advances once per BFS layer, so every source has to be in the initial layer. Starting from one source makes later sources appear to start late and inflates the count.

options.text: Because BFS cannot be restarted
options.why: BFS can be restarted; the problem is that a restart would count its minutes separately rather than in step with the others.

options.text: Because the queue must be non-empty to begin
options.why: A single source would also make the queue non-empty. The issue is the timing of the other sources, not emptiness.

options.text: Because DFS would be needed otherwise
options.why: DFS is the wrong tool here regardless — it explores depth-first and does not track layers, which is exactly what the minute count requires.

leetcode.prompt: In the longest-substring-without-repeats problem, why is jumping the left pointer to lastSeen + 1 better than advancing it one step at a time?

options.text: It removes an inner loop and keeps the whole solution O(n)
options.why: Correct. Crawling left forward re-examines characters already known to be inside the window, which can degrade to O(n²). The jump makes each pointer traverse the string once.

options.text: It uses less memory
options.why: Memory is the same either way — a map of last-seen indices, bounded by the alphabet size.

options.text: It handles Unicode correctly
options.why: Neither approach addresses Unicode; that depends on how the string is indexed, not on the pointer strategy.

options.text: It is required for correctness
options.why: Crawling is still correct, just slower. The difference is complexity, not correctness.

leetcode.prompt: Kahn's algorithm finishes having emitted fewer nodes than the graph contains. What does that mean?

options.text: The graph contains a cycle
options.why: Correct. Nodes inside a cycle never reach in-degree zero, so they are never enqueued. Comparing the emitted count against the node count is the cycle test.

options.text: The graph is disconnected
options.why: Disconnected components are fine — Kahn's starts from every in-degree-zero node, so separate components are all emitted.

options.text: The adjacency list was built backwards
options.why: That would produce a wrong order, not a short one. Reversed edges still eventually drain in an acyclic graph.

options.text: The queue was a stack instead
options.why: Using a stack changes which valid topological order you get, not how many nodes come out.

java.prompt: Which map guarantees iteration in the order keys were first inserted?

options.text: LinkedHashMap
options.why: Correct. It maintains a doubly-linked list across entries in insertion order, which is exactly what it adds over HashMap.

options.text: HashMap
options.why: HashMap makes no ordering guarantee at all. Any order you observe is an artefact of hashing and can change when the map resizes.

options.text: TreeMap
options.why: TreeMap iterates in key order — natural ordering or a comparator — not insertion order.

options.text: Hashtable
options.why: Hashtable is the legacy synchronised map and, like HashMap, guarantees no ordering.

java.prompt: Why is HashMap unsafe under concurrent writes even when no two threads touch the same key?

options.text: A concurrent resize can corrupt internal structure regardless of which keys are involved
options.why: Correct. Rehashing rebuilds the table, and two threads resizing at once can leave entries lost or, historically, in a cycle. Key disjointness does not help because the table itself is shared.

options.text: It is safe as long as the keys differ
options.why: That reasoning ignores the shared table. Resizing touches every bucket, not just the one for your key.

options.text: Only reads are unsafe
options.why: Reads alone are safe. It is the concurrent structural modification that breaks the invariants.

options.text: It throws ConcurrentModificationException in that case
options.why: That exception is for iteration during modification. Concurrent writes fail silently instead, which is worse.

java.prompt: What does a Java stream do when a terminal operation is never called?

options.text: Nothing — intermediate operations are lazy and never run
options.why: Correct. Intermediate operations only build a pipeline. Without a terminal operation nothing is consumed and no element is processed.

options.text: It processes all elements eagerly
options.why: That is the behaviour of a plain loop, not of a stream. Streams defer everything to the terminal stage.

options.text: It throws IllegalStateException
options.why: That is thrown when a stream is reused after being consumed, not when it is never consumed.

options.text: It processes the first element only
options.why: No element is processed. Short-circuiting is a property of some terminal operations, which is a different thing.

java.prompt: An object is used as a HashMap key. Its hashCode is overridden but equals is not. What happens?

options.text: Lookups fail even for an equal object, because equality falls back to reference identity
options.why: Correct. The bucket is found by hash, but the entry is confirmed by equals. Default equals compares references, so a distinct-but-equal instance never matches.

options.text: It works, because hashCode alone identifies the entry
options.why: Hash collisions are expected, so the map must confirm with equals. Hash alone cannot identify an entry.

options.text: It throws at insertion time
options.why: Nothing throws. The map behaves consistently by its own contract; it is your contract that is broken.

options.text: The map silently uses toString instead
options.why: toString has no role in map lookup.

java.prompt: What distinguishes a checked exception from an unchecked one in Java?

options.text: Checked exceptions must be declared or handled at compile time
options.why: Correct. Anything extending Exception but not RuntimeException must be caught or declared, and the compiler enforces it.

options.text: Checked exceptions are slower to throw
options.why: Throwing cost is the same. The difference is entirely a compile-time contract.

options.text: Unchecked exceptions cannot be caught
options.why: They can be caught normally; they simply are not required to be.

options.text: Checked exceptions cannot cross thread boundaries
options.why: Neither kind crosses threads implicitly — an exception is confined to the thread that threw it, whatever its category.

aws.prompt: Which S3 storage class is designed for data accessed roughly once a quarter with millisecond retrieval?

options.text: S3 Standard-IA
options.why: Correct. Infrequent Access keeps millisecond retrieval while lowering storage cost, in exchange for a retrieval fee and a 30-day minimum duration.

options.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
options.why: Deep Archive retrieval is measured in hours, which rules out any millisecond requirement.

options.text: S3 Standard
options.why: Standard would work but costs more per GB with no retrieval fee — the wrong trade for quarterly access.

options.text: S3 Express One Zone
options.why: Express One Zone targets single-digit-millisecond, very high request rates, which is the opposite access pattern.

aws.prompt: An EC2 instance in a private subnet needs outbound internet access but must not be reachable from it. What provides this?

options.text: A NAT gateway in a public subnet
options.why: Correct. NAT translates outbound traffic and holds no inbound route back to the instance, which is exactly the asymmetry required.

options.text: An internet gateway attached to the private subnet
options.why: Attaching an internet gateway route makes the subnet public by definition, which is the thing being avoided.

options.text: A security group rule allowing outbound only
options.why: Security groups filter traffic but do not provide a route. Without a route to the internet there is nothing to filter.

options.text: A VPC endpoint
options.why: Endpoints reach specific AWS services privately. They do not provide general internet egress.

aws.prompt: An explicit Deny in one policy and an Allow in another apply to the same action. What is the result?

options.text: Denied — an explicit Deny always wins
options.why: Correct. Evaluation is deny-by-default, an Allow can override the default, and an explicit Deny overrides everything. That ordering is what makes guardrail policies work.

options.text: Allowed — the more specific policy wins
options.why: Specificity plays no part in IAM evaluation. The three-step order is absolute.

options.text: Allowed — identity policies beat resource policies
options.why: Neither type outranks the other. An explicit Deny in either is final.

options.text: It depends on policy attachment order
options.why: Policies are evaluated as a set. Attachment order is not part of the model.

aws.prompt: A standard SQS queue delivers the same message twice. Is this a defect?

options.text: No — standard queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent
options.why: Correct. Duplicates are a documented property of the standard queue. FIFO queues offer exactly-once processing within a deduplication window when that guarantee is required.

options.text: Yes — SQS guarantees exactly-once delivery
options.why: Only FIFO queues offer exactly-once processing, and only within a deduplication interval. Standard queues never promise it.

options.text: Yes, if the visibility timeout is set correctly
options.why: A correct visibility timeout reduces redelivery from slow consumers, but duplicates remain possible by design.

options.text: No, but only when the queue is encrypted
options.why: Encryption has no bearing on delivery semantics.

aws.prompt: What most directly reduces cold-start latency for a Java Lambda function?

options.text: Provisioned concurrency
options.why: Correct. It keeps initialised execution environments warm, which removes the JVM start and class-loading cost from the request path.

options.text: Increasing the timeout
options.why: Timeout caps how long an invocation may run. It has no effect on how long initialisation takes.

options.text: Adding more environment variables
options.why: Environment variables do not affect initialisation time in any meaningful way.

options.text: Switching to a larger deployment package
options.why: A larger package makes cold starts worse, not better, since more must be loaded.
